region.en: From Winter's ice-house to Summer's warm tent (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自冬之冰屋至夏之暖帳（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 3. Coyote and the Geese' (Winter's war on Summer)

summary.en: Winter, insulted by the meat Summer's people threw at her, resolved to wage war on Summer; her four sisters drove her away with a stick and refused to go, so the old giant and his youngest daughter set out alone on a white bob-tailed horse made of ice, with ice-spears, ice-arrows and ice hanging all over their bodies. Summer saw a fog coming and knew what it was; when the girl told him they were close by, he shook his blanket — the deer's liver and lungs his daughter used — and all the ice melted and fell off their bodies. 'You have no power. Take all the meat you want,' said Summer, and they loaded their horse and went home.
summary.zh: 冬女受夏族擲肉之辱，誓師征夏。四姊以棍驅之，拒不從行。冬神乃與幼女獨往：乘冰製白短尾馬，携冰矛冰箭，周身掛冰。夏神見霧氣而來，已知其故；聞女報『敵至』，抖動其毯（其女所用鹿肝肺）——冰甲盡融墜地。夏神曰：『爾等已無能為。要肉便拿去。』父女載肉而歸。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Season-war myth closing the Winter/Summer episode. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The girl returned home and found her father sitting in the house; she threw the meat at him, just as Summer had done to her, and he picked it up likewise and ate it. He decided, however, to wage war on Summer, and told his youngest daughter to summon her sisters. They drove her away with a stick, and refused to go; therefore the giant and his youngest daughter prepared to go without them. They took a white bob-tailed horse made of ice, ice-spears, and ice-arrows; ice was hanging all over their bodies. They came to Summer's house, the girl riding behind the old man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 148 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Summer saw a fog, and knew what was coming. When his daughter told him that they were close by, he shook his blanket — the little girl used a deer's liver, the old man a deer's lungs, to drive them away — and all the ice melted and fell off from their bodies. When they came nearer, Summer said to them, 'You have no power. Take all the meat you want.' They loaded their horse and went home. That is the end of the story.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 148 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Swallowing Monster of Kamiah

region.en: Kamiah on the Clearwater, monster's body across the valley (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 清水河卡米亞，魔軀橫跨河谷（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 4. Coyote and the Swallowing Monster'

summary.en: Coyote ties himself with wild grape-vine in three places, hides behind a bundle of grass with pitch and fire-sticks in his quiver, and challenges the monster Iltswe'tsix at Kamiah: 'Let us swallow each other!' Drawn in against his ropes, breaking one after another, he insists on entering by the mouth — tramples Rattlesnake flat-nosed for not biting the monster, reproaches Grizzly-Bear for not killing him — and reaching the hanging heart, stabs it, builds a fire under it, and orders the people to step out before the monster dies, himself last. The monster may be seen at Kamiah to-day, and the heart is there too.
summary.zh: 郊狼以野葡萄藤三處縛身，以草束遮身潛近卡米亞之魔 Iltswe'tsix，挑戰曰：『吾倆互吞如何！』魔吸之，藤索逐一崩斷；郊狼堅持自其口而入——踩扁響尾蛇之鼻（斥其不噬魔）、叱灰熊不誅魔——終至懸心之處，以刀刺之，於心下燃火，令眾人於魔死前奪路而出，己則殿後。卡米亞至今猶見魔之遺骸，其心亦在。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Monster-slaying culture-hero cycle; a second version places the monster on Salmon River. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote came back westward through Idaho. On his way he heard that a monster was swallowing the people. Coyote tied himself with a wild grape-vine in three different places, and then crawled over the mountains to see the monster. He hid behind a bundle of grass that he carried in front of himself; he had pitch and fire-sticks in his quiver. He met the monster at Kamiah, and then he mocked him, saying, 'Iltswe'tsix — that was the monster's name — let us swallow each other!' The monster was so surprised that he did not know what to say. He told Coyote to swallow him first; Coyote said that he preferred him to begin, but finally he gave in and agreed to swallow the monster first.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 148-149 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote drew in his breath, and the monster could hardly withstand the suction: 'Doggone you! you are stronger than I thought.' Coyote then said, 'Now it is your turn.' The monster tried hard to move Coyote, but he was tied fast; Coyote then tried a second time, and was able to move the monster a little. When the monster tried again, one of the ropes that held Coyote broke; the next time all the ropes broke, and Coyote was drawn towards the monster. He argued with him, because they could not agree on the way Coyote should enter his body: the monster tried to get him to go in through the anus or the ears; Coyote insisted on going in through the mouth, and at last the monster consented. He opened his mouth, and Coyote went in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 149 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Inside he met Rattlesnake, who wanted to bite him; Coyote trampled him under foot, thereby flattening his nose, and reviled him for not biting the monster. Farther in he met Grizzly-Bear, and reproached him for not killing the monster. Finally he reached the place where the monster's heart was hanging; he stabbed it with his knife. The monster now tried to coax Coyote to come out, but he refused, and proceeded to build a fire directly under the heart; then he cut it. He ordered the people to get ready to step out before the monster should die; they went out, Coyote last of all. The monster may be seen at Kamiah to-day, and the heart is there too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 149 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Butchers the Monster: The Making of the Tribes

region.en: Butchering-place of the monster at Kamiah (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡米亞魔屍剖分之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 4. Coyote and the Swallowing Monster' (the division of the body)

summary.en: Coyote decided to cut up the monster and divide it among the people: out of its feet he made the Blackfeet; the Crow, the Sioux, and the Bannock were all made out of different parts of its body. Asked what he took for himself, he answered, 'To be wise (?).' Then he called for water, washed his hands and scattered the water, saying, 'You shall be the Nez Perces, a small tribe, but you shall be the most powerful of all the people.' In the second version he threw the skin to Montana — 'This shall be the Blackfoot Indians, and they shall be tall, stout men' — made the tribes from the other parts, and when Fox objected that he had done nothing for the place where they were living, sprinkled the blood left on his hands and on the ground: 'This blood shall be Indians in the future. They shall be good warriors and strong, but they shall be few in number.' These were the Nez Perce Indians.
summary.zh: 郊狼剖魔分肉：以其足造黑腳人；烏鴉、蘇人、班諾克各族，皆取魔身不同部位而成。人問其自取何物，答曰：『取智（？）。』復索水洗手上之血，將水潑灑，曰：『爾等將為內茲珀斯人，族小人少，然為萬族中最強者。』另一異文：皮擲蒙大拿——『是為黑腳人，身長體壯』——餘體分造諸族。狐嫌其未為本地居民做任何事，郊狼遂將手上與地上之血灑於斯：『此血將化為印第安人，勇敢強健，然人數不多。』是即內茲珀斯人。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Dismemberment ethnogony parallel (Ymir/Pangu/Purusha cluster). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Then Coyote decided to cut up the monster and to divide it among the people. Out of its feet he made the Blackfeet. The Crow, the Sioux, and the Bannock were all made out of different parts of its body. While Coyote was standing there, some one said, 'What did you take yourself?' and he replied, 'To be wise (?).' Then he called for water. He washed his hands and scattered the water, saying, 'You shall be the Nez Perces, a small tribe, but you shall be the most powerful of all the people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 149 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the second version Coyote now began to butcher the monster. He threw the skin to Montana, and said, 'This shall be the Blackfoot Indians, and they shall be tall, stout men.' The other parts of the body he threw in different directions, and thus made the different tribes. After the body had been entirely dismembered, Fox, who was watching him, said, 'You have done nothing for the place where we are now living.' There was some blood left on his hands and on the ground; Coyote sprinkled it over the place, saying, 'This blood shall be Indians in the future. They shall be good warriors and strong, but they shall be few in number.' These were the Nez Perce Indians.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 151 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote's Wars: The Humming-Birds of the Canyon

region.en: Canyon ridge with the two white heart-sticks (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 峽谷山脊，雙白心柱所在（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 5. Coyote's Wars' (the Humming-Birds)

summary.en: Two Humming-Birds, the only living things about, challenge Coyote — 'Let us have war!' — kill him and throw him into the river; he drifts ashore where Magpie pecks his eyes awake. 'I was just dreaming about getting some girls at the head of the canyon,' says Coyote; Magpie tells him those birds were put there when the world was first made, and teaches the secret: their hearts are two white sticks with two white feathers on the hill-top — seize the poles, break the feathers, and they die. Transformed into an old man, Coyote baits them — 'Come down and kill me' — slips up the other side, reaches the poles with the birds almost upon him, breaks the feathers, and kills both: 'Hereafter you shall just be pretty little birds, and not kill people.'
summary.zh: 兩蜂鳥乃當地唯一生靈，向郊狼挑戰：『來戰！』殺之而投諸河。其屍漂至岸邊，喜鵲啄其目而醒。郊狼曰：『吾方夢見峽源之美女。』鵲告之：此二鳥乃開天闢地時所置，專司殺人；欲誅之，須奪其命根——山頂兩根白柱，上各插白羽，是即其心。化為老翁誘敵：『來殺我吧！』趁其下谷，反向山頂疾奔，搶得木柱，折其白羽——二鳥遂死。郊狼曰：『爾等從此只為小鳥，不得再殺人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. First of the Coyote's-wars episodes. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling upstream. He heard a noise like the sawing of wood, and stood still and listened: two Humming-Birds were there, the only living things about. They said to Coyote, 'Let us have war!' Coyote heard them, and, throwing his bow and arrow down in front of him, replied, 'That is what I have been looking for, a light.' With that he jumped about, ran up the ridge toward them; and they came down the canyon, and rushed at him from both sides. They killed Coyote, and told him that he was to be nothing but Coyote. They dragged him to the river and threw him into the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 151 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He floated down the stream until his body drifted ashore. Magpie saw him lying dead, and began pecking at his eyes, which awakened Coyote. 'That is not right. I was just dreaming about getting some girls at the head of the canyon,' he said to Magpie, who replied, 'There are two Humming-Birds up there who kill everybody, and they are the ones who killed you. They were put there when the world was first made. Listen to what I tell you now! Return the way you came. Make yourself an old man, and, should they say anything to you, tell them to kill you because you are tired. When they come up over the hill, there will be two white sticks with two white feathers on them on the top of the hill. These are their hearts. Take the canyon trail and run as hard as you can toward the sticks; keep going until you get them. Then take hold of the poles, break the feathers, and thus kill them. That is the only way to destroy them.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 152 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He transformed himself into an old man and went off, in accordance with Magpie's instructions. He met the Humming-Birds, who said, 'Let us have war!' — 'Come down and kill me,' was Coyote's reply as he lay down on his back. When they started towards him, he ran up on the other side, and was half way up when they got down. They turned, and saw that he was fairly close to the two poles, and started after him. When he reached the two poles, they had almost caught up with him; he seized the poles, however, broke the feathers, and thus killed both of them. Then Coyote said to the Humming-Birds, 'There are other people coming. Hereafter you shall just be pretty little birds, and not kill people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 152 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Bluff above the river where the forked-stick woman waits (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 河上峭壁，分叉木杖女子伏擊處（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 5. Coyote's Wars' (the mountain-sheep woman)

summary.en: A handsome girl with a forked white stick calls travellers to come and lie with her, then bids them look down at a big mountain-sheep and pierces their necks with the forked stick as they stoop, pushing them over and into the river. Magpie revives Coyote a second time and tells him the woman has always been there to kill everybody: when she calls again, climb up, ask her for the stick because you are tired, and push her over. Coyote does so — 'Now, grandchild, show me where to look' — and knocks her head off as she looks down. 'That is easy; but hereafter when people come, they shall eat you, for from now on you shall only be a mountain-sheep.'
summary.zh: 一美貌少女持白色分叉木杖，喚旅人曰：『來與吾同臥！』待其近前，又令其俯視崖下大角羊；趁其彎腰，以杖刺其頸，推落河中。郊狼二度為喜鵲所救。鵲曰：『此女常伏於此殺人。』教其計策：她再喚時，登崖索杖——『吾倦矣』——趁其俯視，推其下崖。郊狼依計而行，一刀擊落其首。臨終言：『此事易耳。然自此以後，人將食爾——爾已化為凡獸大角羊矣。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: He continued his journey up the river. Soon he heard a woman: 'Whoever you are, come and lie with me!' When he came up to her, he saw that she was a handsome girl, with in her hand a forked white stick. Coyote asked, 'Grandchild, what do you want?' She told him to look down, and he would see a big mountain-sheep. As he stooped down to do so, she pierced his neck with her forked stick, pushed him over, and killed him. She went to see whom she had killed, and saw that it was Coyote; she was afraid that his decaying body would smell, so she threw it into the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 152 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: It floated down and drifted ashore at the same place as before. Magpie pecked at his eyes and cured him. Coyote told him that he was dreaming about some woman, and Magpie told him that the woman had always been there to kill everybody: 'When she does so again, climb up to her; and when she tells you to look, ask her to come down because you are tired. Then push her over and kill her. She is a mountain-sheep.' Coyote went up, listened, and heard her calling him; he climbed up and pretended to be tired, and asked her for the stick. 'Now, grandchild,' he said, 'show me where to look.' She stepped to the bluff; and when she looked down, he knocked her head off and killed her. 'That is easy,' he said, 'but hereafter when people come, they shall eat you, for from now on you shall only be a mountain-sheep.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 152 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mussel Girl and the Leech Woman

region.en: Spring-side opening on the river bank (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 河畔泉邊空地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 5. Coyote's Wars' (the Mussel and the Leech)

summary.en: A fine-dressed girl on the hillside calls 'Come and lie down with me!' — and when Coyote obeys, her sexual organs bite and kill him. Magpie names her the Mussel and teaches the remedy: a notched bone to pry her open. Killed in turn, she is dragged to the river: 'You shall never move about again. You shall be called Mussel, and people shall eat you.' Farther up, a fat girl with red paint on her dress can say only 'U u u!' and 'E e e!'; she chokes Coyote with her grip and throws him in. Magpie names her the Leech and tells Coyote to make a big fire and push her into it; crawling out, she is pushed back and killed — 'Sometimes you will get on to children and crawl into them, but not many will die from your bites. Good people are coming, and you shall not harm them.'
summary.zh: 衣飾華美之少女立於坡上，呼曰：『來同臥！』郊狼從之，竟為其下體咬斃。喜鵲告之：此乃蚌女，當以帶齒之骨撬之。郊狼依計誅之，棄屍於河：『爾從此不得移動，名為蚌，人將食爾。』再上，遇一肥女，裙染紅彩，唯能發『嗚嗚』之聲；抱郊狼至窒息，擲之於河。鵲名之為螞蟥，授計以大火焚之。郊狼積薪燃火，以長棍推之入火；她爬出，再推，遂斃。郊狼曰：『爾偶附孩童爬入其身，然死者無多。善人將至，不得害之。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote now resumed his way upstream. It was not long before he met a woman who called him: 'Come and lie down with me!' He looked at her, and saw that she wore a fine dress down to her waist; the girl stood on the hillside. Coyote climbed up to her, and asked her what she had said. 'Lie with me,' was the answer. When he obeyed, her sexual organs bit and killed him. The girl then dragged him to the river and threw him in, as the others had done. He floated down to the same place as on the previous occasions, and Magpie found him and revived him. 'You brown-eye!' Coyote said, 'why are you running about here? I was just getting some girls from the head of the canyon.' — 'That was the Mussel who killed you,' Magpie said. 'Go back and take a bone with notches in it, and then, when she lies down, run it into her and pry her open.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 152-153 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote went back, and the girl called to him as before, 'Come and try me, whoever it is that is going up there!' Coyote went to her and killed her, as instructed by Magpie. Then he dragged her to the river and threw her in, saying, 'You shall never move about again. You shall be called Mussel, and people shall eat you. Soon other people will come.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 153 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went on up the stream. He came to an opening where he saw a fat girl; she had red paint on her dress. Coyote asked her, 'Why are you sitting there?' All she answered was, 'U u u!' — she could not say anything else. Coyote then thought he would take her along. 'Must I carry you on my back?' Her reply was, 'E e e!' He lifted her up; and when he was ready to put her down, he said to her, 'Let go! Here is a good place to stop.' The girl, however, only tightened her hold until she choked Coyote. She recognized him, and threw him into the river, and Magpie revived him as before. 'That was a leech,' Magpie told him. 'When you go back, she will be there. Ask her if she is cold, and she will say, E e e! Then make a big fire, take a stick, and burn her.' Coyote went up, reached the woman, and said to her, 'My cousin, I see you are still here. Are you not cold sitting in the spring?' — 'E e e!' was her answer. He gathered a load of wood and made a big fire; then he pulled her toward it, and with a long stick pushed her in. When she tried to crawl out, he pushed her back and killed her. Then he said, 'Your name shall be Leech. Sometimes you will get on to children and crawl into them, but not many will die from your bites. Good people are coming, and you shall not harm them.' That was the end of Coyote's journey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 153 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and Crane: The Stingy Fisherman

region.en: Middle of the current where the long-legged fisherman stands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 長腿漁夫立於急流中央（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 7. Coyote and Crane'

summary.en: A long-legged man stands in the middle of the current catching fish with a long pole, a pile of fish on the bank; twice Coyote asks for a fish and is refused — the second time mocked with his own words. When the man starts to ford the river, the angry Coyote throws a rock that breaks his legs, and he floats down the river repeating 'Your load was too heavy and broke your legs!' until only bubbles rise. 'Henceforth you shall be a crane, and people shall make fun of you. From now on, when a man kills much game, he shall give others some.'
summary.zh: 長腿漁夫立於急流中央，以長竿捕魚，岸邊魚積如山。郊狼兩度乞魚，均遭拒絕，且受其嘲弄。漁夫涉水而返之際，郊狼怒擲石塊，斷其雙腿；漁夫順流而下，口中喃喃：『負荷太重，腿為之折！』終至滅頂，唯見氣泡。郊狼曰：『從今為鶴，任人取笑。此後凡獵得多者，當分與他人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote continued his travels up the river, and met a man with long legs, who stood in the middle of the current, catching fish with a long pole; a pile of fish lay on the bank of the river. Coyote spoke to him, but the man did not answer; he kept on catching fish, which he strung up. Coyote asked him for a fish, but his request was refused. He asked a second time, and this time the man mocked him, repeating Coyote's words: 'Give me one.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 155 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: After a while the man started to ford the river. Coyote, who was very angry, threw a rock at him, hit his legs, and broke them. The man floated down the river; and Coyote called after him, 'Your load was too heavy and broke your legs!' The man repeated the words after him. As he was sinking, Coyote spoke again; but when the man tried to answer, all that could be seen were bubbles on the surface of the water. Coyote said, 'Henceforth you shall be a crane (mu'k'a), and people shall make fun of you. From now on, when a man kills much game, he shall give others some.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 155 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Eye-Juggler: Coyote Loses His Eyes

region.en: Woods where Wildcat plays ball with his eyes (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 野貓戲眼之林（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 8. The Eye-Juggler'

summary.en: Hearing some one sing 'Come back, my eyes!', Coyote finds Wildcat playing ball with his eyes and resolves to try; his first eye drops back into its socket when called, but Wildcat, knowing it is Coyote, knocks the eye aside with his horn so it does not return. Taking out the other so that 'both will come back to me,' he throws them both at once — Wildcat knocks both away, and Coyote becomes totally blind. He comes to a tent where an old woman sings that it is a good thing Coyote lost his eyes; he kills her, skins her, eats the meal and seeds, and assumes her shape. The grand-daughters who dance about Coyote's eyes come home, the youngest alone recognizing him; they carry 'grandmother' to the dance, each elder dropping her in turn at his touch, until at the dance he demands his eyes, puts back his own, throws off the disguise and scatters black paint behind him five times to darken the pursuers' way until, weary, they give up — and Coyote got his eyes back.
summary.zh: 郊狼聞歌『回來吧，吾眼！』見野貓以眼為球而戲，羨而效之。拋出之眼一呼即回；然野貓識其為郊狼，以其角擊偏其眼，使之不返。郊狼自以為：『取出另一眼，二眼皆歸。』雙拋之際，野貓又擊——郊狼全盲。行至一帳，老嫗歌唱『郊狼失眼，真是好事』；郊狼殺之、剝其皮、食其糧、披其衣，假扮老嫗。其眾孫女自郊狼之眼舞會歸來，唯幼女識破。眾女輪流背『祖母』赴會，長者皆因被他觸碰而棄之；至會場，郊狼索回己眼，褪去偽裝而逃，沿途五次撒黑漆遮蔽追者，眾人疲而罷追——郊狼復得雙眼。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Eye-juggler cycle. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and heard some one singing, 'Come back, my eyes!' Soon he saw Wildcat playing ball with his eyes. He said, 'I wish I could do that! If I could do that and do it at Qualp, I should do great things.' Coyote decided to try; he went into the woods, and when he tried to take out his eye, it hurt so that he screamed. Finally he succeeded in removing it; he threw it up into the air and called to it to come back, and it dropped back into its socket. 'Now I can do it,' he said to himself. Wildcat heard him, and, knowing it was Coyote, took his horn, and, when Coyote threw his eye up again, knocked it out of the way, so that it did not return. Coyote called several times, but the eye did not come back. Coyote now said, 'My eye must be near. If I take out the other one, they will both come back to me.' So he took it out and threw it up; both came back. 'That's a fine trick,' Coyote said. Now he threw both at the same time; this time Wildcat knocked both away, and Coyote became totally blind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 155-156 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Coyote came to a tent, he found an old woman living there. He listened outside, and heard her sing about Coyote's eyes: 'It is a good thing he lost his eyes.' Coyote went in and saw the woman grinding seeds very fine. 'What are you singing about?' — 'Coyote lost his eyes. That is why I am singing. People are gathered here from all over, dancing about Coyote's eyes. My grand-daughters have gone there. They will come back to me soon.' The woman then gave some seeds to Coyote, who said to himself, 'I must kill this old woman.' 'I must go out a minute,' he told her, went out to get two stones, returned, said, 'I am glad Coyote lost his eyes,' and hit her on the head with a stone, killing her. He took his knife and skinned her, hid the body outside, cooked and ate all the meal and seeds, then put on her skin and clothes and assumed her shape, keeping on pounding the meal and seeds until towards evening.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 156 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The oldest daughter came in, then the next younger, and the others in order, the youngest one coming last. She looked at Coyote and recognized him, and decided that he had killed her grandmother; the other girls rebuked him for not grinding the seeds properly — 'The meal is much too coarse' — and he answered, 'My legs hurt. I was shot in the thigh a long time ago, and it hurts so that I cannot do much pounding now.' The girls went back into the tent, and, being tired, went to sleep. Coyote put his hand on the privates of the four elder girls; as he approached the youngest, she awoke and kicked him, knowing he was Coyote: 'What are you doing?' At this the other girls awoke too, and rebuked her for acting so toward her grandmother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 156 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The following day they said to her, 'Grandmother, they want you at the dance to dance about Coyote.' — 'I am so weak, I doubt if I could get there.' — 'We will carry you,' the girls said. The oldest one carried him first; Coyote told her to raise up her dress and let him slide down lower on her back, and with that she felt him touch her and dropped him — 'I did not mean to drop her,' she said. The next one tried, and the same thing happened; and so with all four of them. Then they told the youngest that she must do her share, but she refused; when they reached the hill and could see the houses, Coyote said, 'I can walk from here on.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 156-157 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they arrived at the place, they heard a loud noise and saw the people dancing, and there was another Coyote at the camp. This one, when he caught sight of them, called out, 'The old woman is coming to dance with us!' The disguised Coyote began to dance and sing, and forgot all about his lameness. 'Where are Coyote's eyes? Let me have them!' he said. 'Let her have them!' some one said; the people crowded together and made room for her to dance. As soon as he had his eyes, he took out the other ones and put back his own; then he took off his disguise and ran away. The people wondered at first, then saw they had been deceived, and pursued him. Fox caught up with him; Coyote then scattered some of the black paint that he had, and it grew dark. The pursuers lost their way, while Coyote sat on a hill a little way off; when it cleared, they gave chase again, and Coyote eluded them as before. This happened five times. At last they grew weary and gave up the chase. So Coyote got his eyes back. Later on he went back and gave names to the children of the girls whom he had deceived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 157 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Rival Suitors: The False Accusation

region.en: Hunters' lodge, then the tree climbed to the sky (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 獵戶之宅，繼而通天之樹（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 9. The Rival Suitors' (the false accusation)

summary.en: The younger of two great hunter brothers, making arrows by the fire, is called out by his sister-in-law to shoot a little bird for her; while he is gone she scratches her own face with the bird's claws and lies accusing him — but the grizzly-bear dog saw everything. The elder brother breaks the boy's arrows in the fire; the boy takes his bow and wanders off with the dog, crosses five mountains, undresses, and climbs a tree higher and higher until out of sight — he climbed into the sky and entered Spider's house, never coming back. The dog howls at the tree-foot for days; the repentant brother crosses three mountains to find it, learns the whole truth from the bear-dog, and leaves him there: 'You shall be a grizzly bear. You shall kill people when you must, but not always. I shall go home and kill my wife, and then go to the village to live.' Walaetitsa shoots his wife and swallows all his fine things, becoming small and extremely ugly.
summary.zh: 獵戶兄弟中，弟於火旁製箭，嫂喚其出射小鳥；乘其在外，嫂以鳥爪自抓其面，誣其非禮——然灰熊犬目睹一切。兄折其箭投火；弟携弓與犬出走，越五重山，脫衣攀樹，愈攀愈高，直至不見——入天界蜘蛛之屋，永不復返。犬於樹下日夜悲嚎。兄自責，越三山尋至，從灰熊犬口中得知真相，留之於山中：『汝當為灰熊。必不得已時方可殺人。吾將歸而誅吾妻，再往村中居住。』瓦萊提察射殺其妻，吞盡其珍寶，變得又矮又醜。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. First half of the rival-suitors cycle. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was the leading man in a certain village; Eagle was the second in rank. There were two brothers who lived some distance away. They were great hunters and very wealthy, honored by all, but preferring to live by themselves. The older one was married; his name was Walaetitsa, his wife's name Ti'pti'-ptle'ya (a small bird). The younger one had a dog, the Grizzly-Bear, who was in love with the younger brother, though he paid no attention to her. One day the younger man said to his brother, 'My arrows are broken, I want to get some wood for shafts. You may go hunting alone to-day.' The elder brother set out by himself; the younger one cut sticks, made several arrows, and put them near the fire to dry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 157 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: While he was working, his sister-in-law called him from outside: 'Come out and shoot this little bird for me!' He refused, saying, 'Why do you want the bird?' She coaxed him; and finally he went out, shot the bird with a broken arrow, and threw it at her, saying, 'There is the bird. What do you want it for?' Then he went in. Soon he came out again to cut more arrow-sticks; while he was gone, his sister-in-law went in and scratched her face with the claws of the bird, then lay down. The young man's dog saw the whole performance. When her husband came home and saw her lying there, he asked what ailed her; finally she replied impatiently, 'See what your brother has done to me! He tried to force me; and when I resisted, he scratched my face.' The grizzly-bear dog lay there and watched, and heard everything. The man turned around, and, seeing the boy's arrows, broke them and threw them into the fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 157-158 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The young man came in and asked, 'Where are my arrows?' No one answered; then he saw the ends in the fire. Finally his brother spoke, and said, 'So you did not want to go out hunting this morning, did you? You wanted to force your sister-in-law.' The boy got up, took his bow and arrows, and went out, his dog following him; he left the house and wandered off on his travels. He crossed five mountains; the fifth mountain was very high. Here he undressed, and told the dog to stay below and wait, while he climbed a tree, higher and higher until he was out of sight — he climbed into the sky and entered Spider's house, and never came back. The dog waited at the foot of the tree several days, howling all the time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 158 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: His brother now began to reproach himself: 'What have I done? I have wronged my brother.' He went out and followed his trail, and when he had crossed three of the mountains, he heard the dog howling; crossing the fourth, the sound became much more distinct, and soon he came to the place where the dog was. He approached him, and the dog growled, acting as if it wanted to kill the man, until Walaetitsa begged and begged: 'O dog! where is your master?' The dog at last replied, 'You cruel man! You have done wrong. My master has left me, and I am here alone... He has ascended the tree, saying he would not come back. He has gone for good.' Walaetitsa asked how it all happened, and the dog gave an account of everything — how the wife had scratched her own face, and how his master had done no wrong. 'If that is so, I shall leave you here as a grizzly bear. You shall kill people when you must, but not always. I shall go home and kill my wife, and then go to the village to live.' With that they parted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 158-159 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Walaetitsa approached his home, and saw his wife outside dressing a skin. He drew his bow and arrow and aimed at her. 'Are you going to shoot me?' she asked him, laughing. He did not answer, but merely drew his bow and killed her. Then he went into the house, swallowed all his fine things, and went to the village. Walaetitsa was a rather large man; but when he had swallowed all those things, he became very small and extremely ugly — he and his brother had been the best-looking men in the village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 159 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
